Series::log1p¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::log1p() const -> Series
Series& Series::log1p_()

What It Does¶

log1p() applies log(1 + x) elementwise.

That one added 1 matters conceptually. The method is not the same thing as plain log(): it shifts the domain and changes the slope.

For real-valued use, the expression lives on the real line only when 1 + x is positive, which is why values near -1 deserve attention.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, containing log(1 + x) lane by lane.

Gradient¶

If y = log(1 + x), then:

  • dy/dx = 1 / (1 + x)

So with the scalar objective L = sum(y), each lane’s contribution is the reciprocal of 1 + x_i.

In-Place Form¶

log1p_() is the in-place sibling of log1p(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.log1p_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.69314718]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. The forward values reflect log(1 + x), not log(x).

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-0.5, 0.0, 3.0}).log1p() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.69314718, 0, 1.3862944]

Example 2. The reverse pass uses 1 / (1 + x) lane by lane.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.log1p();
y.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.69314718, 1.3862944]
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0.5, 0.25]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • log1p() is not interchangeable with log().

  • The slope steepens as x approaches -1 from the right because 1 / (1 + x) grows there.

  • This is an elementwise transform only; there are no axis or keepdim toggles.

Summary¶

Use log1p() when the natural logarithm should be applied after shifting the input by one.

See Also¶

  • Series::log: plain natural logarithm.

  • Series::expm1: exponential-minus-one counterpart.
